newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Ambroveneto, Cariplo link in bank shakeup.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Ambroveneto, Cariplo link in bank shakeup.

text.p: Banco Ambrosiano Veneto on Wednesday approved a merger with Cariplo, creating Italy's biggest banking group in terms of the number of branches, gross operating profit and capacity to generate revenue.

Ambroveneto said in a statement the new private group would be the country's second biggest in terms of assets, deposits and loans after Istituto Bancario San Paolo di Torino. It will be the number one banking group in the country based on gross operating profit, which totalled 3.045 trillion lire ($1.7 billion) based on end-1996 figures.
The new group will have a total of 1,822 branches, or a national market share of 7.5 percent, well ahead of rivals.
The new combine, already dubbed AmbroCariplo by the media, will have assets of 252 trillion lire, deposits of 157 trillion lire and just under 35,000 employees.

Italy's largest savings bank Cariplo -- whose full name is Cassa di Risparmio delle Provincie Lombarde -- was founded in 1823, while Banco Ambrosiano Veneto came about in the 1989 merger of Nuovo Banco Ambrosiano and Banca Cattolica del Veneto.
Banking sources said that, while the new group would tower over most of its Italian rivals, it remained a relatively small operation in the European context.

The government has urged Italian banks, regarded as inefficient and overmanned by European standards, to merge with each other and streamline activities in preparation for the planned launched of a single European currency in 1999.
To fund the merger, Ambroveneto said it would make a capital increase of around 6.5 trillion lire and issue some 2.0 trillion lire worth of convertible bonds.

Giuseppe Guzzetti, chairman of the charitable foundation that controls Cariplo, told a news conference on Wednesday the new group would have a syndicate pact of major shareholders in place for five years.
The foundation formally approved the merger on Tuesday.

After the formal creation of the new group, which does not yet have a name, the major shareholders will include France's Credit Agricole with 30 percent, the Cariplo foundation with 22 percent and Italian insurer Alleanza with eight percent.
Ambroveneto chairman Giovanni Bazoli underlined the "solidarity and stability of Ambroveneto shareholders" in supporting the merger project.

The operation is based on an estimated total value of Cariplo at end-1996 of 10.3 trillion lire, less 1.68 trillion lire worth of the bank's shareholding and real estate assets that will be hived off into a separate company to be controlled by Cariplo's foundation.
The capital increase and formal purchase of Cariplo is expected to be closed by the end of this year, while the merger will take five years to be fully completed.
